episodes.episode_title: Ep 23: Alberta voters rejected a break with Canada, and Premier Smith calls it a reset with Ottawa.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **Alberta voters rejected a break with Canada, and Premier Smith calls it a reset with Ottawa.**

**What You Need to Know:** Alberta voters rejected a break with Canada, and Premier Danielle Smith calls the result a reset with Ottawa. The Globe and Mail reported an emphatic rejection of a separatist push for a permanent rupture, other premiers welcomed that loss, and some First Nations leaders said ballot delays left communities out of a vote they saw as touching treaty rights. In the United States, a presidential super PAC is spending heavily in the midterm stretch, while Ottawa has a deportation order against a Toronto man over Iran sanctions evasion.

### Lead
**Danielle Smith calls for unity after separatism rejected in Alberta referendum: Global News**
Alberta voters rejected an effort by separatists to pursue a permanent rupture with Canada, The Globe and Mail reported. Premier Danielle Smith hailed the referendum results as a reset with Ottawa. A day after voters rejected the idea of further pursuing separation, Smith delivered a message on where the province goes from here, Global News reported. Other premiers welcomed the separatist loss and largely steered clear of other ballot questions on immigration, judges and the Senate, The Globe and Mail reported. Some Indigenous leaders criticized delays and a lack of ballots, saying the province failed to appreciate their communities’ interest in a vote many saw as affecting treaty rights. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12110203/alberta-referendum-danielle-smith-results-speech/) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-politics-insider-a-great-day-for-canada-as-alberta-chooses-unity/) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-premiers-welcome-separatist-loss-in-alberta-referendum/) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-alberta-referendum-first-nations-lack-of-ballots-delays/) Source: [cbc.ca](http://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7389521)

### Across the Region
**Trump Wields an Unprecedented $277 Million in Final Midterm Stretch: The New York Times**
President Donald Trump’s super PAC is putting 277 million dollars into the final midterm stretch, spending The New York Times says has no parallel in American history. The paper says that sum could offer struggling Republican candidates a lifeline. MAGA Inc. is flooding social media with targeted ads aimed at turning out Republicans amid what The New York Times calls the president’s historically low approval ratings. The spending is the term-limited president’s. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/trump-maga-inc-midterms.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/trump-maga-inc-super-pac.html)

**FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service: NPR**
The Federal Aviation Administration has cleared the way for airlines to put Boeing’s 737 Max 10 into service, NPR reported. Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in bringing the plane to airlines. The clearance is a step toward service for a jet NPR describes as long-delayed. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/21/g-s1-149032/faa-boeing-737-max-10)

**In San Francisco, a Family Earning $325,000 Qualifies for Government Aid: The New York Times**
San Francisco is subsidizing child care for high-income households as an artificial-intelligence boom drives up prices, The New York Times reported. A family earning 325,000 dollars qualifies for that government aid. Even with the subsidy, families say they are struggling. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/san-francisco-cost-living-affordable-housing.html)

### The Closer Look
**Canada orders deportation of Toronto man who helped Iran evade sanctions: Global News**
Canada is ordering the deportation of Amin Yousefijam, a former Tehran police lieutenant living in Toronto, after the Immigration and Refugee Board found he played an important and critical role in a crime group that helped Iran evade sanctions. The 36-page decision, released to Global News on Tuesday, says the Iranian citizen, in Canada since 2016, was the group’s logistician and oversaw shipping for a transnational procurement operation. Global News reported that the electronics, motors and other materials he exported were dual-use, with civilian and military applications, and could be harnessed to manufacture weapons of mass destruction. Board member Christopher Marcinkiewicz wrote that Yousefijam belonged to an organization whose criminal activity directly contravened Canadian and U.S. sanctions on certain exports to Iran, and wrote, “I issue a deportation order against him.”

Yousefijam arrived from Tehran a decade ago under the name Amin Riki. He was arrested in Toronto in 2021, extradited to Michigan to face allegations tied to a sanctions-evasion gang led by his brother Arash, pleaded guilty, and was deported to Ontario, where he took a third name, Ameen Cohen. The board found he intentionally failed to declare that U.S. conviction on an Ontario legal name-change form, rejecting his claim that a government employee told him foreign convictions need not be reported, and called the omission the conduct of someone who will say whatever serves his immediate purpose. Hearings ran from September 2024 to February 2025. The order was issued in July 2026 and released to Global News this week. Marcinkiewicz wrote that Yousefijam joined voluntarily, knowing he meant to defeat sanctions, and that a more limited role than his brother’s was still critical because it focused on shipping sanctioned goods from the United States to Iran.

Yousefijam told Global News he was still in Canada, would not say whether he had appealed, and said he was considering his options while the minister had options of their own. “Right now I’m just, you know, living my life peacefully,” he said. The Canada Border Services Agency did not answer Global News by deadline. The report places the case amid Ottawa’s effort to expel members of Iran’s regime: senior Iranian officials were banned in 2022, and as of October 1 the border agency said it had found 40 top-level regime officials in Canadian cities, with two deported, eight gone voluntarily, two awaiting removal, and the rest before the board or already through hearings. Global News also reported last month that the son of Iran’s former vice president has lived in Edmonton as Sal Ghafouri, received almost 2 million dollars in federal contracts, and is under investigation over alleged work for Iran’s military. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12109602/canada-deport-toronto-iran-sanctions-evasion/)

### Also Today
**Trump Says He Asked Putin to Release an American Jailed in Russia: The New York Times**
President Donald Trump said he asked Vladimir Putin to release Stephen James Hubbard, a Michigan teacher seized from his home in Ukraine months after Russia invaded. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/trump-russia-prisoner-stephen-hubbard.html)

**Lawsuit challenging Trump's tariffs against Canada filed in U.S. Court of International Trade: CBC**
A lawsuit challenging President Trump’s tariffs against Canada has been filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/trump-tariffs-lawsuit-9.7388900)

**Carney government has no launch date planned for proposed sovereign wealth fund: CBC**
Nearly six months after announcing a Canadian sovereign wealth fund, the federal government still has no launch date and is not sure how the fund will work. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/sovereign-wealth-fund-update-9.7387449?cmp=rss)

**Justice Kagan warns Supreme Court rulings are fueling polarization and undermining democracy: AP News**
Justice Elena Kagan warned that Supreme Court rulings are fueling polarization and undermining democracy. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/supreme-court-democracy-elena-kagan-4554d6c508f37ac9821dfed06cfa02ab)

**Victims of Wainwright fire remembered as young people dedicated to service: The Globe and Mail**
A fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured 39 others. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-wainwright-fire-victims-remembered-young-people-dedicated-service/)

**Florida gambling helpline director sentenced to nearly 10 years over $1.4m theft to fund addiction: The Guardian US**
Philip Sullivan, who later directed Florida’s gambling-addiction helpline, was sentenced to nearly ten years after a conviction for stealing 1.4 million dollars from Royal American, a Panama City Beach real-estate firm where he was chief financial officer. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/21/florida-gambling-director-jailed-addiction)

**Gabby Thomas, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and the doping tensions dividing sprinting: The Guardian US**
After finishing second to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Olympic 200-metre champion Gabby Thomas said, “I am an equal-opportunity doping hater,” and said she was not naming anyone. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/oct/21/gabby-thomas-melissa-jefferson-wooden-dennis-mitchell-doping-sprinting)

**53 Nevada legislative seats are up in 2026. Most fundraising is going to nine of them.: The Nevada Independent**
Of 53 Nevada legislative seats on the 2026 ballot, most fundraising is going to nine of them. Source: [thenevadaindependent.com](https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/53-nevada-legislative-seats-are-up-in-2026-most-fundraising-is-going-to-nine-of-them)

**Some on DOJ's 20,000 "likely" noncitizen list in Calif. appear to be U.S.-born: NPR**
Los Angeles County election officials say a preliminary look at a Justice Department list of 20,000 “likely” noncitizens registered to vote in California shows the list is unreliable, and some names appear to be U.S.-born. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/20/nx-s1-6009873/california-doj-voter-rolls-noncitizens)

### The Region and the World
**Carney’s Turkish balancing act must include business, defence and human rights: CBC**
Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to Turkey to seek closer trade, energy and defence ties with a NATO ally, CBC reported. The visit is described as a turnaround after relations soured under a Canadian arms embargo. Ankara’s crackdown on dissent is the test of Carney’s promise to balance economic pragmatism with Canadian values. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/carney-trade-defence-turkey-human-rights-9.7389188?cmp=rss)

### Both Sides: British Columbia's $10-a-day child care
British Columbia votes on Saturday with a signature child-care promise still short of what the B.C. NDP pledged. The question is whether the province should keep a pause on the $10-a-day program into at least early 2027, or put new money in now.

The case for waiting comes from Education and Child Care Minister Lisa Beare, who told The Globe and Mail the program as structured is not sustainable at $10 a day because there is not enough money in the system. The province paused it in February until at least early 2027. Spaces at $10 a day are about 10 percent of licensed spaces, the $10aDay Child Care Campaign says, and just over 17,000 program spaces exist against a July 2021 promise, under the Canada-wide agreement, of 30,000 new affordable spaces within five years and an average of $10 a day by March 2026.

The case for pushing ahead is that families outside the program still pay some of the country’s highest fees, and that scarcity is the failure. Sharon Gregson of the Coalition of Childcare Advocates of B.C. said new spaces, a 50 percent fee cut for publicly funded licensed providers, and higher educator wages are real, and that the government has still not delivered and has stalled. Martha Friendly of the Childcare Resource and Research Unit called the policy a mess and said the question is why there is not more affordable care, after critics attacked Premier David Eby for having a child in a $10-a-day space. A Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives report she co-authored put the median infant fee at 52 dollars a day in Richmond and 40 dollars in Vancouver, against 22 dollars in Toronto and 15 dollars in Calgary. On Saturday the campaigning NDP said that if re-elected it would spend 80 million dollars on 7,200 before- and after-school spaces and 250 million dollars more, with Ottawa, on universal care. Conservative spokesperson Alex Shiff said a Conservative government is fully committed to opening more spaces, available when and where people need them. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-bc-ndp-fallen-short-10-a-day-child-care-commitment-data-suggests/)

episodes.content:
# Omni View North America

> **A judge largely blocked field interviews in nine states over noncitizen voter checks.**

**What You Need to Know:** A ruling has largely blocked homeland security agents from field interviews in nine states, including California, in a search for noncitizens registered to vote. In Toledo, a chemical leak that sent nearly a thousand people out of the area is slowing. In Canada, more than fifty scholars want changes to a signature projects bill, and a new study finds long-term declines in loons.

### Lead
**Judge Restricts D.H.S. Field Operations Aimed at Unearthing Voter Fraud: The New York Times**

A ruling has largely blocked homeland security agents from carrying out field interviews in nine states, including California, the New York Times reports. Those interviews were part of a sprawling effort to find noncitizens registered to vote. The Times describes the block as applying to those field operations, and as large rather than total. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/judge-dhs-voter-fraud-elections.html)

### Across the Region
**Toledo Chemical Leak That Forced Residents to Evacuate Is Slowing: The New York Times**

Nearly 1,000 people in Toledo, Ohio, were told to leave the area, and thousands more were urged to stay inside, the New York Times reports. The leak is slowing. The mayor said the spill did not present a long-term threat. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/toledo-ohio-chemical-explosion.html)

**A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?: NPR**

Republican U.S. Representative David Valadao is fighting for reelection in central California, NPR reports. Six in ten residents of his district are covered by Medicaid, which NPR's headline puts at 62 percent. He voted to cut Medicaid last year. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/22/nx-s1-6002928/republican-congress-midterms-medicaid-cuts-david-valadao-california)

**Some of Canada's top scientists push for changes to Carney's new major projects bill: CBC**

More than 50 of Canada's leading scholars and scientists are urging Parliament to make major changes to a signature bill from Prime Minister Mark Carney's government, CBC reports. They want those changes so fast-tracking projects does not cause irreversible environmental harm. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/royal-society-of-canada-bill-c39-amendments-9.7390486?cmp=rss)

### The Closer Look
**Scientists report ‘substantial’ declines in loons across Canada: The Globe and Mail**

A study published Thursday in the journal FACETS finds substantial long-term declines in loon productivity in all but one of 12 breeding regions. Matthew Fuirst, a research ecologist with Birds Canada who led the work, said loons are not doing as well as researchers would like. More than 20 researchers in Canada and the United States joined a three-year effort that pulled together decades of data.

The steepest declines were in Canada's Atlantic and Prairie provinces, Dr. Fuirst said. Loons are not currently endangered. An estimated 254,000 breeding pairs live in Canada, about 94 percent of the species' total population. The team used more than 45,000 breeding records from 3,421 lakes across North America. About half the data came from volunteers in a long-running Birds Canada loon survey, with some observations reaching back to the 1980s.

Productivity was defined as the number of chicks per adult pair that survive beyond six weeks after hatching. Declines ranged from 0.5 to 2.5 percent a year, over two to four decades depending on the data. Northern Maine was the exception, where productivity has been relatively stable. The northern half of the breeding range is a blind area: fewer people live there, and data have been hard to obtain.

Walter Piper, a co-author and a biology professor at Chapman University in Orange, California, said it was not likely that northern data would show an increase offsetting the south, or that loons were moving farther north. He said the study also indicated a decline in chick quality that could signal poorer nourishment. "We are probably detecting the leading edge of a broad decline in the loon population that is likely to continue in coming decades," Dr. Piper said. Loons are long-lived, he said, so the decline will take a while to become obvious, and causes should be sought now.

One possible cause the researchers flag is increased precipitation linked to climate change. Unlike ducks in some of the same habitat, loons are built to catch fish in relatively clear water, and their bones are denser than those of many other species so they can stay submerged. More flooding and churning of lake water could lower visibility and impede hunting. James Paruk, a loon biologist at St. Joseph's College in Standish, Maine, who was not part of the study, said Maine's stability may reflect relatively low human and shoreline development in the area the study covered. He said the time span and geographic scale make the implications far-reaching. Dr. Fuirst said he has already started a follow-up study on the causes. For many Canadians the bird is tied to wilderness and national identity, including its place on the one-dollar coin. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/science/article-scientists-report-substantial-declines-loons-across-canada-atlantic/)

About 157 million Americans get health insurance through work; an employer survey shows a moderate price uptick this year, and workers still say health costs are a top concern. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/22/nx-s1-6008153/health-insurance-costs-kff-commonwealth)

Stateline reports a record number of women are running for state legislatures this year. Source: [stateline.org](https://stateline.org/2026/10/22/a-record-number-of-women-are-running-for-state-legislatures-this-year/)

**Adoptees from Korea say they were isolated and abused in the US. Were they also ‘stolen’ from their birth parents?: The Guardian**

The Guardian reports that South Korea last year took responsibility for enabling the mass export of children for sale abroad, while Korean adoptees in the United States say they were isolated and abused and are asking whether they were also taken from their birth parents. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/22/korean-american-adoptees)

**Supreme Court to Review Federal Ban on Home Distilleries: The Presidential Prayer Team**

The Supreme Court is to review the federal ban on home distilleries, the Presidential Prayer Team reports. Source: [presidentialprayerteam.org](https://www.presidentialprayerteam.org/2026/10/22/supreme-court-to-review-federal-ban-on-home-distilleries/)

**‘Our hearts beat together’: Wainwright gathers for prayer vigil: Global News**

About 150 people gathered Wednesday night at Wainwright's Church of the Nazarene for a prayer vigil as the community continued to grieve and support those affected. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12112843/our-hearts-beat-together-wainwright-gathers-for-prayer-vigil/)

**Canada’s Carney Turns to Turkey to Diversify Trade and Reduce Reliance on the US: Modern Diplomacy**

Prime Minister Mark Carney is turning to Turkey to diversify trade and reduce reliance on the United States, Modern Diplomacy reports. Source: [moderndiplomacy.eu](https://moderndiplomacy.eu/2026/10/22/canadas-carney-turns-to-turkey-to-diversify-trade-and-reduce-reliance-on-the-us/)

**If Blackburn picks Hegseth to replace her, he'd need GOP permission to run again: Knoxville News Sentinel**

The Knoxville News Sentinel reports that if Blackburn picks Hegseth to replace her, he would need Republican permission to run again. Source: [knoxnews.com](https://www.knoxnews.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/22/if-blackburn-picks-pete-hegseth-senate-he-needs-gop-permission-to-run-again/92363744007/)

### The Region and the World
**U.S. and Israel Draw Up Plans for Renewed Strikes on Iran After Elections: The New York Times**

The United States and Israel are drawing up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the elections, the New York Times reports. The Times says renewed hostilities might not be any more successful than the war's first phase. It also reports that President Trump has repeatedly canceled plans for a return to major combat. episodes.episode_title: Ep 25: Provinces want more say over 91,500 nominee spots that decide who can stay.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **Provinces want more say over 91,500 nominee spots that decide who can stay.**

**What You Need to Know:** Saskatchewan and Newfoundland are pressing Ottawa for more control over immigration, including the 91,500 provincial nominee spots that help decide who can stay in Canada. Alberta voters on Monday backed more provincial say over settlement while rejecting separation. Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab is preparing new permanent-resident targets within weeks, and premiers meet in Ottawa on Monday.

### Lead
**Saskatchewan, Newfoundland push Ottawa for greater control over immigration: The Globe and Mail**
Saskatchewan and Newfoundland are asking Ottawa to hand them more immigration powers, while Alberta renews its demand for greater autonomy over which foreign nationals become permanent residents. The Globe and Mail reports that those demands drew fresh attention after a majority in Alberta voted on Monday for more control over who may settle there. That vote was part of a referendum in which Albertans rejected separating from the rest of Canada and endorsed several measures aimed at curbing inflows of newcomers. Critics warn the shift could produce a fragmented, patchwork system. Federal Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab is preparing to announce within weeks new federal targets for permanent residents, including how many newcomers each province will be able to nominate. Under the Provincial Nominee Program, a province nominates and the federal government ultimately approves who is accepted. The provincial streams are a favoured route for former international students seeking permanent residence. Quebec and Nunavut are the only jurisdictions that do not use the program. In last year’s immigration levels plan, Ottawa set provincial nominee spots at 91,500 people, rising to 92,500 next year. Premiers have been pressing Ms. Metlege Diab to raise the number of permanent-residence spaces available for those nominations. Provinces argue they are best placed to decide which immigrants should settle in order to fill local labour gaps. Saskatchewan’s minister of government relations, Eric Schmalz, said the province will keep pushing for greater control, with the focus on immigrants who can fill job gaps so industries can keep providing jobs for Saskatchewan people and generating revenue for public services. He said that push complements, and does not replace, training more people at home, which he called the first pillar of Saskatchewan’s Labour Market Strategy. Newfoundland and Labrador, through spokesperson Allison King, said it wants both more control and a greater number of nominations, and that it supports increased economic-immigration allocations that reflect each jurisdiction’s labour-market needs. Ms. King said recent reductions under the Immigration Levels Plan constrain the province’s ability to meet employer demand, support rural communities and sustain population growth. She noted immigration is a shared constitutional responsibility, said provincially driven programs have succeeded in attracting and retaining newcomers, growing the population and filling job gaps, and said Newfoundland, as provincial-territorial co-chair of the Forum of Ministers Responsible for Immigration, is working with other governments toward a collaborative approach that recognizes national priorities while giving provinces and territories more flexibility. Prince Edward Island spokesperson April Gallant said the province also supports a greater provincial and territorial role, because provinces deliver health care, housing, schools and roads, understand labour-market needs and the pressure on public services, and should have a meaningful role in shaping levels and programs so allocations reflect workforce demands, economic priorities and population goals. Premiers meet Monday in Ottawa, where greater control over immigration is expected to be raised. At a Wednesday news conference with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said economic immigration is needed to keep economies growing across the board, and that Ontario looks forward to working with the federal government on that. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-saskatchewan-newfoundland-push-ottawa-for-greater-control-over/)

### Across the Region
**Supreme Court Allows Blanket Ban on Student IDs at Polls in New Hampshire: The New York Times**
The US Supreme Court has allowed a blanket ban on student identification at the polls in New Hampshire to stand. The New York Times reports the justices had been asked to weigh a New Hampshire directive that stopped election officials from treating a student ID as proof of a voter’s identity. The court left that restriction in place for officials running those polls. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/22/us/politics/supreme-court-new-hampshire-election-student-id.html)

**US Homeland Security gets go-ahead to test a heat ray for possible border use: Mexico News Daily**
US Homeland Security has received a go-ahead to test a heat ray for possible use along the border with Mexico. Mexico News Daily describes the system as a non-lethal but debilitating weapon. It shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves as far as half a mile. The beam produces an intense burning sensation on human skin. The reported purpose of the test is possible border use, not a deployment already under way. Source: [mexiconewsdaily.com](https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/us-homeland-security-gets-go-ahead-test-heat-ray-for-possible-border-use/)

**Devastating fire at CFB Wainwright started on automatic grenade launcher range, official says: The Globe and Mail**
A devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright began on an automatic grenade launcher range, an official says. The Globe and Mail reports that the head of military police said the fire later spread to a different range in another part of the base. That spread overran soldiers’ positions. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-cfb-wainwright-fire-started-on-automatic-grenade-launcher-range/)

### Also Today
**Carney says AtkinsRealis is a contender to build nuclear power plant in Turkey: eKathimerini.com**

### Both Sides: Whether Canadian outreach counts as US election interference
The question is whether Canadian political contacts inside the United States count as interference in the midterms or as ordinary diplomacy. American voters are preparing to cast ballots in tight midterm elections that, The Globe and Mail reports, will turn on a small number of closely fought races.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s case, made at a news conference in Istanbul on Friday, is that allegations from Donald Trump’s administration have no merit. He said he is disappointed that US ambassador Pete Hoekstra treats making those suggestions as his role, and he called the charges unsubstantiated claims. Canada, he said, keeps a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States, and its hundreds or thousands of interactions are normal efforts by a foreign government to build relations. He said Ottawa has lots of contact with American companies, citizens, individuals and stakeholders, is very careful not to be seen to interfere, and has no intention of interfering with US democratic processes. He said he would not point fingers or get into tit-for-tat, but that there are lots of concerns about American interference in Canadian political processes, and that the media can judge how far very senior US officials have directly made suggestions to intervene in Canadian sovereignty and democratic processes, encourage certain outcomes and encourage certain people. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is rejecting the accusation. She says she would never interfere, because she would expect the Americans not to interfere in Canada’s own elections. Anadolu Ajansı reports that Mr. Carney, while rejecting the interference claims, also said Canada will never be the 51st state.

The US embassy in Canada this week circulated what it called a fact sheet accusing Ottawa of trying to sway US politics. The statement alleges that the Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances. Mr. Hoekstra, in an interview on the Canadian podcast The Really Big Show, said the United States is closely watching Canadian activities, referenced Industry Minister Mélanie Joly among other politicians, and said some of this, from the US view of its elections, could be inferred to be election interference. He cited Ms. Joly talking about targeting retaliatory tariffs in politically sensitive states, and an Ontario government television advertisement that ran in the United States last year criticizing US tariffs on Canadian goods. He said foreign-policy leaders coming into the United States are appreciated, but that they should keep their nose out of American politics, and that Washington is monitoring and evaluating and will respond if it judges the conduct to be election interference. Those remarks followed accusations last month by Trump adviser Peter Navarro, who told Canadian lobbyists to get the hell out of the US and warned Canada against interfering in the midterms. Canada has since warned its diplomats to avoid US candidates, Bloomberg reports, and The Globe and Mail reports diplomats were told not to meet with US midterm candidates. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-carney-in-turkey/) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-joly-pushes-back-on-accusations-of-meddling-in-us-elections/) Source: [bloomberg.com](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-10-22/canada-tells-diplomats-to-avoid-us-candidates-after-trump-interference-claims) Source: [aa.com.tr](https://aa.com.tr/en/americas/carney-rejects-us-election-interference-claims-says-canada-will-never-be-51st-state/4098242)

episodes.episode_title: Ep 26: One lawsuit seeks to block Alaska voters' Senate result if Dan Sullivan loses.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **One lawsuit seeks to block Alaska voters' Senate result if Dan Sullivan loses.**

**What You Need to Know:** The Justice Department has asked a court to block Alaska's Senate result if Republican Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that similar candidate names could taint the count. The New York Times reports that President Trump told the department to intervene, and that legal experts see no obvious authority for stopping certification in advance. The suit is aimed at that race alone.

### Lead
**Trump Officials Seek Block on Alaska Senate Race Results if the Republican Dan Sullivan Loses: The New York Times**
The Justice Department has gone to court over one Senate seat in Alaska, and the remedy it seeks is aimed at the count itself. In what The New York Times calls a highly unusual lawsuit, the department asked to block the state's Senate result if Republican Dan Sullivan loses. The department's stated ground is confusion: candidates with similar names, it argued, could taint the election result. The Times reports that President Trump told the Justice Department to intervene in the race. In a companion account, the Times says polling shows Republicans at risk of losing the seat, and that Trump directed the department in. A separate Times report says legal experts see the challenge as dubious. No obvious legal authority, that report says, supports a pre-emptive effort to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses. The challenge is framed around a narrow loss, not a completed recount the articles describe as already finished. PBS put the same threat on its broadcast, with Jonathan Capehart and Ramesh Ponnuru discussing Trump's threat to block the Alaska election results. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/justice-dept-alaska-senate-race-sullivan.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/politics/alaska-senate-race-explainer.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/alaska-senate-doj-lawsuit-trump.html) Source: [pbs.org](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/capehart-and-ponnuru-on-trumps-threat-to-block-alaska-election-results)

### Across the Region
**How Vivek Ramaswamy’s Ruthless Ad in Ohio Divided Republicans: The New York Times**
In Ohio's race for governor, an attack ad by Vivek Ramaswamy has split Republicans, The New York Times reports. The spot targets his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. The Times calls the advertisement brutal and ruthless, and says the fallout showed that even in the Trump era a political attack can be seen as going too far. President Trump has defended the ad, the Times reports in its election dispatches. Ohio's Republican governor has joined the backlash against it. The dispute is inside the Republican Party over the tone of the spot, not over whether the governor's race is on the ballot. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/us/politics/vivek-ramaswamy-ad-ohio-amy-acton.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/22/us/midterms-elections)

**Justice Dept. Demands That California Counties Help Identify Noncitizen Voters: The New York Times**
The Justice Department has demanded that California counties help identify noncitizen voters, The New York Times reports. Election officials across the state received letters from the agency. The letters say that if they fail to comply, they "risk significant federal scrutiny." The demand is a federal request to county election officials, tied to identifying noncitizen voters, and the consequence named in the letters is scrutiny if the counties do not comply. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/justice-dept-california-noncitizen-voters.html)

**Jeffrey Rath, Mitch Sylvestre said to be fired from Alberta Prosperity Project weeks ago: The Globe and Mail**
Jeffrey Rath and Mitch Sylvestre were removed from the Alberta Prosperity Project weeks ago, The Globe and Mail reports. A movement leader says the pair's removal was for cause. That leader says news of the firing was kept quiet so it would not derail the referendum campaign. The removals, on that account, happened weeks before they became public, and the quiet was a choice made to protect the campaign calendar. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/alberta/article-separatist-leaders-jeffrey-rath-mitch-sylvestre-fired-referendum/)

### The Closer Look
**Tighter immigration rules put nursing homes at risk of losing foreign workers, long-term care providers say: The Globe and Mail**
Nursing homes in several provinces say tighter federal immigration rules now put them at risk of losing significant numbers of temporary foreign workers, The Globe and Mail reports. The homes look after seniors who have cognitive problems or dementia and who need help dressing, bathing, or feeding. Local hiring often falls short, so the homes recruit abroad to fill the gap on those shifts.

Lisa Levin, chief executive of AdvantAge Ontario, which represents the province's municipal and non-profit long-term care homes, said changes Ottawa has made to immigration policy have made a difficult staffing situation in health care worse. Mary Polak, chief executive of the BC Care Providers Association, called the result an unintended consequence. She said the government may not have been aware of the whole scale of the impacts.

The Globe and Mail reports that Ottawa has moved since 2024 to curb the number of international students and temporary foreign workers, after criticism that their influx created housing problems and made it harder for Canadians to find jobs. Levin singled out two measures that hit long-term care. The first is the Labour Market Impact Assessment, the document an employer completes to confirm that no Canadian is available for the job. That assessment is what lets foreign personnel apply for a work permit. Each application carries a $1,000 processing fee. The assessments are now valid for six months, down from a year. The second measure is the work permit itself, shortened from two years to one.

Gavin McIntosh, operations and finance vice-president for The Care Group, which runs nine facilities in British Columbia, said homes are paying overtime to cover the shortages. "It's not sustainable," he said. Levin said other homes have turned to temporary staffing agencies. She said that route is costly, and that it is also detrimental, because vulnerable residents need stable care personnel. "They're working with people who have cognitive issues, and then you have to bring someone else in, you have to train them all over again on what the needs are of the residents," she said. Each resident has a care plan and needs of their own, and in many cases cannot communicate those needs.

The federal government answered that the Temporary Foreign Worker Program should be only a last-resort solution for short-term problems. Samuelle Carbonneau, a spokesperson for Employment and Social Development Canada, said in an email: "It is not a substitute for Canadian talent and is conditional on ensuring that measures have been taken to recruit Canadian workers." She said assessments are not based on job titles. They are assessed individually. She noted that other pathways exist for hiring foreign workers.

One of those pathways is in Quebec. Employers there have a priority process called traitement simplifié that extends to foreign applicants for personal support workers, who provide basic care in nursing homes. Jean-François Blanchard, executive director of two long-term care homes west of Montreal, said some of his foreign candidates have been stumped because that Quebec priority stream does not recognize training they acquired in private establishments. Blanchard, who is also president of a group representing Quebec private nursing homes, said his members could potentially lose 650 of their 6,000 workers because of immigration issues.

Carbonneau pointed to another option: a temporary extension that lets rural employers retain their number of foreign workers until next March. The measure still requires new Labour Market Impact Assessments. Ontario and Alberta are not participating. Ashley Hoffmeister, human resources director for the District of Kenora Homes for the Aged, said 28 of the 400 employees in her three facilities in northwest Ontario are facing expiring papers. She tried another route, the Significant Benefit to Canada permit, commonly known as the LMIA exemption C10. That permit costs $230. The employer has to explain how the foreign workers will make a contribution so significant that they can be exempted from the assessment. Hoffmeister said some C10 applications were turned down because bureaucrats did not recognize the foreign workers as health-care personnel. One rejection letter she shared said the personal support workers "appear to be highly/mainly specific to individual's personal care and not health care." Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-tighter-immigration-rules-put-nursing-homes-at-risk-of-losing-foreign/)

episodes.content:
> **A majority ends nearly a century out of power for British Columbia’s Conservatives, and David Eby resigns.**

**What You Need to Know:** British Columbia’s Conservatives have a majority after nearly a century out of power, and NDP Leader David Eby has resigned after calling the vote early. A shooting near Florida A&M left adults and children wounded, and First Nations leaders meet Canada’s first ministers on Monday. The United States is also moving to lift fifty percent tariffs on some Canadian goods.

### Lead
**British Columbia Conservatives win a majority and David Eby resigns: The Globe and Mail**
After earlier reporting of a narrow race, The Globe and Mail now reports that the British Columbia Conservatives have won a majority government. The paper says the party has returned to power after nearly a century. The Globe and Mail reports that NDP Leader David Eby resigned Saturday night. It says his snap election call backfired. Global News reports that British Columbians voted on October 24. Global News reports that the provincial election had been set to take place in 2028. David Eby called the snap election rather than waiting for that date. A separate Global News report says he called that election in September. The majority means the Conservatives, not the NDP, will form the government. The New Democrats enter that change without Eby as leader. The result closes a campaign that began as an early vote and ended with the governing party’s leader out of office on the night the ballots were counted. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-bc-election-david-eby-ndp-lorne-doerkson-conservatives/) Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12112175/bc-election-results-live-numbers-2026-vote/) Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12112193/bc-election-2026-find-riding-local-candidates/)

### Across the Region
**At Least 12 Injured, Including 6 Minors, in Shooting Near Florida A&M’s Stadium: The New York Times**
A shooting near Florida A&M University in Tallahassee left people wounded hours after the university’s homecoming game, The New York Times and The Guardian report. The New York Times reports at least twelve injured, including six minors. The New York Times says police said the youngest victim was eleven. The Guardian reports eleven people with gunshot wounds and another person injured. The Guardian says police counted six adults and six juveniles among the injured. Tallahassee police said at least three of the shooting victims had serious injuries. Police said nine others were in stable condition. Police said a physical altercation preceded the gunfire, without elaborating. Police Chief Lawrence Revell said it was especially heartbreaking that children were among the injured. The shooting was on Perry Street on Saturday night. The Guardian, citing the New York Post, said an altercation at a homecoming party escalated into gunfire. That account said a fight between two or three individuals led to shots just before 8 p.m. Police said their violent crimes unit was investigating the circumstances. Florida A&M said on X that the safety and security of students, faculty, and staff remained its highest priority. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/us/tallahassee-shooting-florida-am-homecoming.html) Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/25/eleven-sustain-gunshot-wounds-in-shooting-near-florida-university)

**US seized American heir’s cellphone in violation of treaty agreement, lawyer says: The Guardian**
US authorities seized the cellphone of American activist James “Fergie” Chambers at some point after Spanish police arrested him in July, without notifying him or his attorneys, The Guardian reports. Chambers is a US citizen. He is imprisoned in Madrid. He has applied for asylum as the United States seeks his extradition. The extradition request concerns alleged support for Hamas. The Guardian reports that the case is the first known instance of the United States seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas. The accusation is tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza. The Guardian describes him as a wealthy donor to left-wing and humanitarian projects. His lawyer says the seizure violated a treaty agreement. The allegation is an accusation. The reporting does not describe a conviction. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/25/fbi-spain-james-fergie-chambers-cox)

**A ‘reset’ or ‘one and done’? First Nations and first ministers set to hold historic meeting: CBC**
The Assembly of First Nations national chief says Monday’s meeting with first ministers is a chance to redefine the relationship among First Nations, premiers, and the prime minister, CBC reports. The national chief says that chance exists even though the meeting will take place under a cloud of skepticism. The Globe and Mail reports that the gathering is the first of its kind since 2005. In 2005, premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin met Indigenous leaders in Kelowna, British Columbia. The national chief frames Monday’s session as a possible reset rather than a single meeting with no follow-through. What changes, if anything, depends on whether that redefinition is accepted by the premiers and the prime minister in the room. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/first-nations-first-ministers-meeting-relationship-9.7394258?cmp=rss) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-the-assembly-of-first-nations-prepare-for-historic-meeting-with-carney/)

### Both Sides: Should Berkeley start a public bank with taxpayer dollars?
Berkeley is considering whether to start a public bank with taxpayer dollars, The New York Times reports. The bank would offer low-interest loans to community projects in the East Bay region of Northern California. It remains a proposal the city is weighing, not a statute already in force. No final vote is recorded in today’s reporting.

Proponents say a public bank would allow the city to keep its tax dollars local. Their strongest reason is use of money Berkeley already collects. Those dollars would stay in the East Bay. They would be lent at low interest to community projects, rather than leaving the local economy for outside institutions. Proponents present the bank as a tool for projects the private market may not finance on those terms. The people who would use it, on that account, are East Bay community projects seeking cheaper credit from a city-owned lender.

Opponents say it would be a high-risk experiment with tax dollars. Their strongest reason is exposure. Capitalizing a new public bank with taxpayer money would put public funds at risk if the institution or its loans failed. That loss would fall on the same residents whose taxes supplied the capital. The Times reports that objection as a warning about the experiment, not as a record of a bank that has already failed. The people who would bear it, on that account, are Berkeley taxpayers.

The choice sits with Berkeley’s city government. Proponents are asking it to build a local lender for East Bay projects. Opponents are asking it to keep taxpayer dollars out of that experiment. Today’s reporting does not record a date for a final vote. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/us/berkeley-california-public-bank.html)
